newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Toyota Australia upbeat on sales, profit outlook.
newsitem.headline: Toyota Australia upbeat on sales, profit outlook.

text.p: The Australian manufacturing unit of Japan's Toyota Motor Corp said on Wednesday it was confident of achieving higher sales and increased profits from its domestic operations in the near term.

"We are confident of expanding domestic market sales and improving profitability with the introduction of new models in the next nine months," president and chief executive of Toyota Motor Corp Australia Ltd, Sam Komori, told a luncheon hosted by the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA).
Komori said Toyota was confident of lifting its share of the medium car market after the release of its new Camry model.
"If our experience in the United States (with the new model) is any guide, then our confidence is justified," he said.
Komori said Toyota's production of the new Camry model from its plant in the U.S. state of Kentucky could not meet current levels of demand.
Toyota is one of four major Australian carmakers, the others being Ford Motor Co, General Motors Corp and Mitsubishi Motors.
Toyota Australia's export sales were likely to top A$400 million in calendar 1997, Komori said, and the group expected sales to reach about A$700 million by the year 2000 and top A$1 billion by 2005.
Komori applauded the Australian government's decision last month to hold automotive tariffs at no lower than 15 percent until the year 2005.
"The scene is now set for a period of relative stability for the Australian automotive industry and it will give the industry a chance to consolidate its achievments," he said.

Komori said Toyota Australia could now proceed with a reasonable level of confidence with plant upgrades and expansion and said its parent would now need to seriously consider further investment in Australia.
However, Komori said imported cars would continue to pressure local manufacturers and said the government needed to accelerate its reform of the taxation system.
"We were not alone in calling for an acceleartion of the macro-economic reform process. A clear change of pace is required in the area of wholesale tax," he said.
Komori said the extent to which the Australian car industry could survive was directly related to its international competitiveness.
